html:
The Omagua, also called the Kambeba, are a Tupi-Guarani speaking people of the upper Amazon, today living in small communities in Brazil and Peru. Kambeba means "flat head" in Tupi, after their old custom of shaping infants' heads.

When Francisco de Orellana sailed down the Amazon in 1542, his chronicler described the land of the Omagua as a long, densely settled stretch of river with large villages, fine pottery and powerful chiefs. In the late 1600s the Jesuit Samuel Fritz founded missions among them.

Portuguese slave raids from downriver, Spanish and Portuguese rivalry and epidemics destroyed most Omagua towns in the 1700s. Survivors scattered or merged with others, and their old river land was taken over by peoples such as the Ticuna. Their closest relatives are the Kukama.
